title: No Verified Incident Supports Claims About Vietnam’s Dog Trade
excerpt: No verified incident, court record, seizure, or health alert is available here. Public demands must rest on documented facts, transparent enforcement, and protection for families and animals.
body_html:
Every stolen companion animal represents real family loss. But public outrage must not rest on an unverified raid, conviction, poison attack, or shipment. No specific incident, court judgment, seizure record, or Vietnamese government health alert is documented in the material available for this dispatch.

Evidence must come before accusation

Claims about stolen pets, cyanide bait, illegal transport, “dog farms,” or contaminated meat require primary records: police statements, court decisions, veterinary inspection reports, quarantine documents, or named public-health alerts. Without those records, no honest investigation can claim that every animal in the trade was stolen or that a specific shipment carried disease.

That standard protects Vietnamese families, local investigators, and animals from propaganda. It also protects reform. Criminal theft, unlawful transport, regulatory breaches, lawful activity, and proposed prohibition are different matters. Each needs separate proof and accountability.

Biosecurity still demands hard safeguards

Rabies risk must be described accurately. Infection generally follows infected saliva entering through bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. After possible exposure, wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical assessment. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. WHO guidance supports rapid care before symptoms develop.

Household exposure incidents and commercial supply chains must not be falsely joined. They remain parallel biosecurity concerns: animal movement, quarantine, inspection, and enforcement must protect communities from preventable harm.

Vietnamese leadership can demand transparency

Vietnamese families and communities can lead reform through verified reporting, humane enforcement, pet-theft prevention, quarantine protection, and public disclosure of official findings. The state’s public-health targets are not the same as SDE’s campaign demand for complete abolition.

Sign SDE’s national petition calling for nationwide abolition by 2030. Add your name to a public demand for action—and follow campaign updates on how that demand reaches decision-makers: sign the national petition.
